title: Five percent is a hurdle, not a forecast.
deck: My read after Tuesday's close: a higher discount rate and a potential squeeze on cash flows deserve separate tests. The latest Treasury observation reached 5.00%, but a round number is not a sell signal. The more useful question ahead of the Fed decision is which valuations still work if financing stays expensive and energy costs remain elevated.

sections.title: The curve moved, not just the headline number.
sections.body: Official Treasury par yields for 15 September were 4.67% at two years, 5.00% at ten years and 5.36% at thirty years. Their daily changes were +2, +3 and +2 basis points respectively. The 10Y–2Y spread widened slightly to +33 basis points. My interpretation: this is a modest, broad upward move, not evidence by itself of a sudden regime change. Nominal yields alone cannot tell us how much came from expected policy, real growth, inflation compensation or term premium. Nor is a par-yield observation interchangeable with an intraday bond quote.

sections.title: Weakness was not confined to the Nasdaq.
sections.body: AP's closing figures put the S&P 500 at 7,585.73 (−0.4%), the Dow at 52,093.11 (−0.6%) and the Nasdaq Composite at 25,981.57 (−0.8%). The Russell 2000 also lost 0.8%; all changes are rounded. My read: weakness across these benchmarks merits testing both financing sensitivity and operating assumptions. It does not establish how many individual stocks fell, and one session is not enough to diagnose a recession or identify a single cause.

sections.title: Oil risk belongs in the forecast as well as the discount rate.
sections.body: AP reported Brent's Tuesday settlement at $108.75 per barrel, up 2.9%. Separately, August's CPI release showed headline inflation of 3.4% year-on-year and core inflation of 2.4%, with core prices up 0.3% on the month. These are different time windows: today's oil price is not already measured in August CPI. My inference is conditional: sustained expensive energy could pressure consumers and margins at energy-using businesses, while helping some producers. Pricing power, hedges and demand elasticity determine the company-level impact. A rapid oil reversal would weaken this argument; I would not impose the same earnings haircut on every business.

sections.title: Stress the model before predicting the Fed.
sections.body: The Fed's 15–16 September meeting, including projections, remains unfinished at this cutoff. Expectations are not a policy announcement. In my calculation using this toolkit's fictional default company, increasing WACC from 10% to 11% while holding every other assumption constant reduces estimated value from $15.70 to $13.62 per share, approximately 13.2%. This is a sensitivity illustration, not a forecast for the market: neither a Treasury yield nor a Fed decision maps one-for-one into company WACC. Next test slower cash-flow growth separately, then together with the rate change, to avoid hiding operating risk inside a single discount-rate assumption.

watch: After the 16 September Fed decision, compare the statement and projections with the subsequent bond-market response. Do not assume the headline rate decision alone explains it.
A durable reversal in oil and longer-dated yields would weaken the combined cost-and-valuation pressure thesis; a one-day bounce would be less persuasive.
Look for company evidence of pricing power, demand resilience and manageable refinancing needs. Those would challenge a blanket downgrade to cash-flow forecasts.
